newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Japanese 4x4 -- a must-have for Afghan warlords.
newsitem.headline: Japanese 4x4 -- a must-have for Afghan warlords.

text.p: The most sought-after vehicle is Japanese, the prized footwear is Iranian, the favoured weapons are Russian and the death shroud of choice is fighting clothes with boots on.
The Afghan war, 1997-style, is as international as it has ever been and the only sure winner remains the Grim Reaper.

Throw in always-present tribal rivalries, tense borders with Pakistan, Iran and Uzbekistan, conspiracy theories about oil, all spiced by Islamic fundamentalism, and Afghanistan lives up to its reputation as one of the world's hottest trouble spots.

In the present battle, a so-called northern alliance of ethnic Uzbeks, Tajiks and Hazaras is besieging the capital Kabul, where the purist Islamic Taleban militia rules as the would-be government of this nation of 16 million people.
The siege has dragged on for nearly a month, defying U.N. and other efforts to negotiate an impossible peace in a land where guns are by your side from cradle to grave.
It is a country always in a state of seemingly chaotic mobilisation with soldiers either heading to the front or returning to their villages for rest and recuperation.

Rifles slung on shoulders, small bands of soldiers walk ceaselessly back and forth on roads littered with the debris of tanks, artillery pieces and crashed helicopters from the Soviet army's futile incursion in the 1980s.
A cocked gun pointed at a windscreen is the favourite hitch-hiking method and far more effective than a raised thumb.

The targets are the windscreens of Mercedes-Benz, Hero Benz and Mustang Mercedes -- names drivers have emblazoned on their buses to attract passengers with promises of a trouble-free ride that no vehicle could fulfill on the destroyed roads.
But the fighting man's car of choice in Afghanistan is a Japanese four-wheel drive vehicle, especially Toyota models that carry the myriad "commanders" of the anti-Taleban alliance.
It is the car most often used by alliance leader Ahmad Shah Masood, who is always accompanied by two or three similar black-coloured vehicles manned by heavily armed bodyguards.
Masood also has a Humvee, the U.S. army vehicle that gained prominence in the Gulf War. It is stationed along with several helicopters at his stronghold in the Panjsher Valley.
Masood's bodyguards say their leader rarely uses his Humvee, apparently fearing that a secret tracking device is implanted in its bodywork to let the Americans monitor his movements.
A hero of the battle against the Soviet occupation, Masood is said to meet 200 to 300 people a day in his never-ending negotiations to keep his alliance of guerrillas together.
"We call him 'The Kid'," says a doting foreign-educated press officer, portraying a general who joins his troops to frolic in mountain streams for relief from the seering summer heat.

He has another name -- 'The Bomber' -- for his penchant for blowing up bridges and tunnels to cut off enemy troops or stop them from advancing against his forces. Across some streams in the Panjsher are the remains of three or four previous bridges.
In Afghanistan's landscape of towering mountains, narrow passes and flat plains, height is everything in battle strategy.
"If you are half a metre higher than the other guy, you win," says a Masood aide. "It's that simple."
However, fuel -- or lack of it -- can play havoc with the best-laid plans. Last week the price of fuel doubled overnight after Masood commandeered all supplies in the frontline area.

Uzbekistan, once a key fuel route for opposition forces, has closed its border with Afghanistan for the past few weeks to signal displeasure with the ouster of former northern leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum by his rival, General Abdul Malik.
Soldiers say the fuel shortage has held up Masood's plan to launch his final attack on Kabul to expel the Taleban, a group every opposition fighter believes is supported by Pakistan.
Islamabad denies the charge, but its obvious interest in opening up trade links with landlocked Central Asian republics has given rise to many conspiracy theories.
These involve a role for the Taleban in securing possible routes for pipelines to take oil and gas from Central Asia across Afghanistan to markets in Pakistan, India and beyond.
For the moment, fuel is in very short supply, though a little trickles into opposition-held territory from Iran.

Iranian army boots are also hot items. When a truckload of them arrived at the front line last week, soldiers who normally make do with tattered sandals rushed for the boots and had to be kept at bay by guards posted around the truck.
On the frontline, when the fighting and shelling briefly die down at night, the only sport is scorpion-throwing.

A visiting team of foreign journalists fared badly, failing even to take the field when they fled their mud hut after a group of good-natured but raucous soldiers threw several of the venomous creatures into their midst.
